tagline: Through Luck and Trust, a creek-side road reaches Hot Springs.
intro: Appalachian Medley runs through forests and mountain coves before opening into a valley, with Pisgah National Forest closely bordering the route. North of Betsy’s Gap, the drive follows Spring Creek toward Hot Springs, where the creek meets the French Broad River. NCDOT’s scenic-byway guide presents the journey through the area’s musical history and wooded hills, listing 43 miles and a drive time of one hour and 15 minutes.

At Hot Springs, earlier travelers included drovers taking cattle, hogs and horses to markets in South Carolina and Georgia. Construction of the Buncombe Turnpike through town in 1828 made the springs more accessible. The railroad arrived in 1882, while resort hotels rose and burned: the Warm Springs Hotel burned in 1884 and its successor, the Mountain Park, was built in 1886. The Appalachian Trail now follows Bridge Street through downtown.

Start on NC 209 at I-40 Exit 24 near Lake Junaluska and head north toward Betsy’s Gap. Hebo Mountain lies south of the gap and Pug Knob north; beyond them, Spring Creek accompanies the road through Luck and Trust toward Hot Springs. Continue on US 25/70 to Walnut, where the guidebook’s route ends at Walnut Drive.

moments.title: Betsy’s Gap
moments.text: At Betsy’s Gap, the mountains have names on either side of the road: Hebo Mountain to the south and Pug Knob to the north. From this point north, the byway follows Spring Creek. The creek flows through Pisgah National Forest along much of its lower course and joins the French Broad River in Hot Springs. Luck is a few miles beyond the gap, with Trust farther north on NC 209.

moments.title: Trust
moments.text: Trust sits north of Luck at the junction of NC 63 and NC 209, spreading along Spring and Friezeland creeks. The origin of its name is obscure, though NCDOT’s guidebook records the local saying “with Luck comes Trust.” The guide places the communities a mile or so apart and identifies St. Jude’s Chapel of Hope as a landmark in Trust. It credits the chapel to a local woman and recounts her recovery from a terminal illness.

moments.title: Hot Springs
moments.text: The name changed when a hotter spring was found: Warm Springs became Hot Springs in 1886. The town occupies the meeting of Spring Creek and the French Broad River. Its resort buildings changed repeatedly, too. The Warm Springs Hotel burned in 1884, and the Mountain Park Hotel followed in 1886. In 1917, the U.S. government leased the hotel and grounds for an internment camp that held German and Austro-Hungarian civilians. That hotel burned in 1920. Another travel route now passes through town: the Appalachian Trail follows Bridge Street and climbs the mountains on both sides of the river.
